         LINEARITY OF NON-ABELIAN TENSOR SQUARES: A
           COUNTEREXAMPLE AND THE BRAID GROUPS

                                         GROUPTHEORY50


        Abstract. We answer both parts of Kourovka Problem 19.9. First, for r ≥ 4 the
        finitely generated linear group Sp2r (Z) has a non-linear non-abelian tensor square,
        by combining the Brown–Loday description for perfect groups with Deligne’s non-
        residually finite universal central extension. Second, for every n > 3 the tensor square
        Bn ⊗ Bn of the braid group is linear. The latter follows from the homology map
        H2 (Bn ; Z) → H2 (Sn ; Z) and the standard splitting of the tensor square when the
        abelianization has no 2-torsion.




                                        1. Introduction
  Brown and Loday introduced the non-abelian tensor product and related it to low-
dimensional homotopy and group homology [5]. Bardakov, Lavrenov and Neshchadim
showed that linearity of G alone does not force linearity of G ⊗ G, using non-finitely-
generated examples, and isolated the finitely generated case as an open problem [3].
This became Kourovka Problem 19.9: if G is finitely generated and linear, must G ⊗ G
be linear, and in particular what happens for braid groups Bn , n > 3 [7]?
  We show that the general answer is negative but the braid-group answer is positive.

                      2. A finitely generated counterexample
  For a group G there is an exact sequence
                                                         κ
                                                  → G′ −→ 1.
                               H2 (G; Z) −→ G ∧ G −
If G is perfect, then G ⊗ G = G ∧ G and this is the universal central extension of G [5].
Theorem 2.1. There is a finitely generated linear group G such that G ⊗ G is not linear.
Proof. Take
                                     G = Sp2r (Z),           r ≥ 4.
This group is finitely generated, perfect, and linear. In this range the pullback of the
universal cover of Sp2r (R) is the universal central extension

                                   1 −→ Z −→ G
                                             e −→ G −→ 1

[1]. Deligne proved that every finite quotient of Ge kills a nonzero multiple of the central
generator; in particular Ge is not residually finite [6].
   Since G is perfect, Brown–Loday gives G ⊗ G ∼    = G.e A finitely generated linear group
is residually finite by Mal’cev’s theorem. Therefore G ⊗ G cannot be linear.              □

universal central extension.

                                        3. The braid groups
     Let n ≥ 4 and let
                                   β : Bn ↠ Sn
be the standard epimorphism with kernel the pure braid group Pn . We use
                 B ab ∼
                      = Z,
                         n
                                         ∼ C2 ,
                             H2 (Bn ; Z) =        H2 (Sn ; Z) ∼
                                                              = C2 .
Lemma 3.1. The induced map
                                    β∗ : H2 (Bn ; Z) −→ H2 (Sn ; Z)
is an isomorphism.
Proof. The five-term sequence for
                                       1 → Pn → Bn → Sn → 1
contains
               H2 (Bn ) → H2 (Sn ) → H1 (Pn )Sn → H1 (Bn ) → H1 (Sn ) → 0.
The coinvariants H1 (Pn )Sn are infinite cyclic because Sn is transitive on the standard pure-
braid generators Aij . The class of A12 = σ12 maps to twice the generator of H1 (Bn ) ∼  = Z.
Hence the map H1 (Pn )Sn → H1 (Bn ) is injective. Therefore H2 (Bn ) → H2 (Sn ) is
surjective, and since both groups have order two, it is an isomorphism.                     □
     Put An = Sn′ = Altn and define the pullback
                                       En = Bn′ ×An (Sn ∧ Sn ).
Proposition 3.2. The natural map Bn ∧ Bn → En is an isomorphism.
Proof. Both groups are central extensions of Bn′ . The induced map is the identity on
the quotient, while on the kernels it is precisely the isomorphism of Lemma 3.1. The
short five lemma gives the result.                                                  □
Theorem 3.3. For every n > 3, the non-abelian tensor square Bn ⊗ Bn is linear.
Proof. The group Sn ∧ Sn is finite. The group Bn′ is linear because Bn is linear by the
theorems of Bigelow and Krammer [4, 8]. Hence the pullback En , as a subgroup of
Bn′ × (Sn ∧ Sn ), is linear. Proposition 3.2 therefore shows that Bn ∧ Bn is linear.
   Since Bnab ∼
              = Z has no 2-torsion, the splitting theorem for non-abelian tensor squares
gives
                Bn ⊗ Bn ∼  = ∇(Bn ) × (Bn ∧ Bn ),              ∼ Γ(Z) ∼
                                                        ∇(Bn ) =      =Z
[2]. Thus Bn ⊗ Bn is a direct product of linear groups and is linear.                 □

                                            4. Conclusion
   The two parts of Problem 19.9 exhibit genuinely different behavior: finite generation
does not rescue tensor-square linearity in general, while braid groups retain linearity
after passage to the non-abelian tensor square.
